head: A Vermeer that has been missing since 1990.
sub: The Concert was stolen from Boston's Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum on March 18, 1990. It has never been found.
caption: Vermeer painted this trio of musicians in a Delft interior around 1664: a woman at the keyboard, a man with a lute, a woman singing. It is thought to be the most valuable stolen work still unrecovered. Look for the viola da gamba lying on the floor, waiting for a player who never comes.

caption: A young woman strums a guitar and glances away to one side, as if someone just out of frame is listening. Thieves took the painting from Kenwood in 1974 and demanded a ransom before it was recovered. It has hung there since the Iveagh Bequest in the 1920s.
credit: Johannes Vermeer, The Guitar Player, c. 1672 · Kenwood House, London (Iveagh Bequest) · Public domain

head: A family portrait, and everyone has an instrument.

sub: Johann Christian Bach, youngest son of J. S. Bach, sat for Gainsborough in 1776. He died in London on January 1, 1782.
caption: Bach first asked Gainsborough to paint him for Giovanni Battista Martini's gallery of musicians in Bologna, then ordered this second version for himself. head: Goya's largest etching: a blind guitarist and his crowd.
sub: Around 1778 Goya etched his design for a royal tapestry, which the weavers found too complex. It is his only print after one of his own paintings.

caption: The kithara was the lyre used for public performance, including epic poetry. On the other side of this Athenian amphora stands a judge with his wand, so the scene is probably a competition. Look at the long robe and the instrument's heavy wooden arms.
credit: Attributed to the Berlin Painter, Terracotta amphora, c. 490 BCE · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · CC0
audio: Mesomedes of Crete, Hymn to the Sun (lyre and voice)
facts_checked: Attributed to the Berlin Painter, ca. 490 BCE; obverse young man singing and playing the kithara, used in public performance incl. epic recitation; reverse judge identified by garb and wand; probably a competition -> https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/works-of-art/56.171.38
notes: Portrait, 2978x3722, CC0. Screenshot confirmed this file shows the kithara side. Black glaze; best on dark background.

sub: The Escorial 'Codex of the Musicians' of the Cantigas de Santa Maria, early 1280s, has 41 miniatures of musicians, most in pairs.

head: The poet called 'Praise of Ladies', with his band.
sub: Heinrich Frauenlob sits on a high seat with a staff, while a crowd of musicians plays below. From the Codex Manesse, Zurich, about 1304 to 1340.
caption: The Codex Manesse collects German love songs with full-page pictures of their poets. Frauenlob's page is a whole concert: find the fiddler in the middle, plus pipes, a drum and more. Legend says the women of Mainz carried his coffin to the cathedral in 1318.
credit: Codex Manesse, Meister Heinrich Frauenlob (fol. 399r), Zurich, c. 1304 to 1340 · Heidelberg University Library · Public domain

notes: Portrait, 2020x2804. Instruments read from the image (fiddle center, pipes, drum); curator please confirm. 'Legend says' keeps the bier story hedged as Wikipedia does ('It is said').

head: Six musicians and one dancing boy, Korea, 1700s.
sub: Kim Hong-do painted everyday Joseon life. Here a sextet of two pipes, a flute, a haegeum fiddle and two drums plays for a boy in mid-dance.
caption: Kim Hong-do, known by his art name Danwon, is famous for his album of genre scenes. The players sit in a half circle around the dancer. Find the haegeum, a two-string fiddle, and the hourglass drum.
credit: Kim Hong-do, A Dancing Boy (Album of Genre Paintings), late 18th century · National Museum of Korea · Public domain
audio: Traditional Korean, Sujecheon (court ensemble)

head: The drone that holds Indian music together.
sub: A court lady from Kishangarh in Rajasthan plays the tanpura, the long-necked lute that sounds the steady drone under a raga. About 1735.
caption: The Met describes her as a nayika, the ideal heroine of devotional poetry, with hints of Radha, Krishna's beloved. Her jewels and fine clothes mark her as a member of the court. Look at her fingers on the strings and the big round gourd resting at her lap.
credit: A Lady Playing the Tanpura, Kishangarh, Rajasthan, c. 1735 · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain
audio: Traditional, Raga Yaman alap (voice with tanpura)
facts_checked: Title, ca. 1735, Rajasthan, Kishangarh, 1996.100.1; nayika; plays a tanpura; elaborate jewelry marks her as court member; alludes to Radha -> https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/38038
notes: Portrait, 2148x3408. The 'drone' role of the tanpura is general music knowledge, not from the Met page; curator may wish to add a source.

head: Chant without staff lines, St. Gallen, around 922.
sub: The Cantatorium of St. Gallen is called the earliest complete surviving music manuscript written in neumes.
caption: A monk at the abbey of St. Gallen wrote out the soloist's chants of the Mass between about 922 and 926. There are no staff lines: small neumes above the words show how the melody moves.
credit: Anonymous scribe, Cantatorium (Cod. Sang. 359), Introit and Gradual, c. 922-926 · Abbey Library of St. Gallen · Public domain
audio: Anonymous, Gregorian chant Ad te levavi (unaccompanied voice)

head: Paris, around 1200: Pérotin's Alleluia Nativitas.
sub: A student known as Anonymous IV listed this three-voice piece among the works of 'Magister Perotinus' of the Notre Dame school.
caption: Pérotin worked in Paris around 1200 and is counted the leading composer of the Notre Dame school of polyphony. Almost all we know of him comes from that late 13th-century English student. This copy is in a manuscript at the Herzog August Bibliothek in Wolfenbüttel, Germany.
credit: Pérotin, Alleluia Nativitas, Codex Guelf. 1099, manuscript copy · Herzog August Bibliothek, Wolfenbüttel · Public domain
audio: Pérotin, Alleluia Nativitas (three voices)
facts_checked: Pérotin active around 1200, most important member of the Notre Dame school; known mainly through Anonymous IV, who names Alleluia Nativitas and calls him Magister Perotinus; it is a three-voice piece -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pérotin
Image is Alleluia nativitas from Codex Guelf. 1099, source diglib.hab.de (Herzog August Bibliothek) -> https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Perotin_-_Alleluia_nativitas.jpg
notes: 1400x2400, PD. Portrait page. Not to be confused with Pérotin's Christmas organum Viderunt omnes; this is a different piece, so no Christmas date.

head: A dance in paint, and the dance song below it.
sub: Machaut's Remède de Fortune includes one piece in each lyric genre. On this page a round dance is painted above the song 'Dame, a vous sans retollir'.
caption: Guillaume de Machaut oversaw the making of manuscripts of his complete works. In the Remède de Fortune the story itself calls this song a chanson baladee, a dance song. Look for the castle at left, the dancers under the trees, and the red staff lines of the music below.

head: The blind organist of Florence, in a golden initial.
sub: This page of the Squarcialupi Codex has an initial believed to portray Francesco Landini, blind from childhood after smallpox.
caption: The codex was made in Florence around 1410 to 1415 and holds 354 Italian songs. Landini has 146 complete pieces in it, the largest surviving collection of his music. Each composer's section opens with an illuminated portrait.

Landini blind from childhood after smallpox; died 2 September 1397; tombstone shows a portative organ -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Landini

head: The oldest surviving keyboard music, around 1360.

caption: The fragment comes from Robertsbridge in East Sussex and is now in the British Library. Its six pieces are three estampies, a dance form, and three arrangements of motets. This leaf begins 'Tribum, quem non abhorruit'; look for the letters written under the staff.

Fol. 44r shows the beginning of 'Tribum, quem non abhorruit' -> https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Robertsbridgecodex_fol44r.jpg

head: Barbara Strozzi, Venice, 1659: Opus 7.
sub: Strozzi published eight volumes of her own music and was called the most prolific composer, man or woman, of printed secular vocal music in mid-1600s Venice.
caption: Diporti di Euterpe, 'Euterpe's pastimes', is her Opus 7. The poet Giulio Strozzi, who called her his adoptive daughter, founded an academy that staged performances at their home. This copy is at the Library of Congress.

head: Handy sold The Memphis Blues. This 1913 edition added words.

head: Fauré's Dolly Suite, written for a little girl's birthdays.
sub: Fauré wrote the six pieces of Dolly, Op. 56, for piano duet between 1893 and 1896, to mark events in the life of Emma Bardac's daughter.

head: Satie's golf piece: no bar lines, and a colonel in loud tweed.
sub: Satie wrote the 21 tiny pieces of Sports et divertissements in 1914, in his own calligraphy, for an album illustrated by Charles Martin.
